01.note: Rabbi Tarfon treated his mother with remarkable devotion: whenever she wanted to climb into her bed, he bent down so she could step up on him, and whenever she got down, she stepped down onto him. He came to the study hall and praised himself for honoring his mother so thoroughly. The Sages there told him he had not reached even half the honor due to her, and asked him: has she ever thrown a purse into the sea in front of you, and you did not embarrass her?
01.why: The Gemara is collecting examples of how far the duty to honor parents goes, after Avimi stood over his sleeping father; this story shows that even extraordinary service can fall short of the full measure.

people.name: Rabbi Tarfon
people.about: A Sage who served his mother by letting her step on him to get in and out of bed, and boasted of it in the study hall.

terms.meaning: A commandment of the Torah; here, the commandment to honor one's father and mother.

02.note: Rav Asi's elderly mother asked him for jewelry, and he made it for her. She asked for a husband, and he said he would look for one. When she asked for a husband as handsome as he was, he left her and went to the Land of Israel. Hearing that she was following him, he asked Rabbi Yohanan whether he could leave the Land to go meet his mother. Rabbi Yohanan said he did not know, and later said: Asi, you are determined to leave; may the Omnipresent return you in peace. Rabbi Elazar assured the worried Rav Asi that this was a blessing, not anger. Meanwhile Rav Asi heard that her coffin was coming, and said: Had I known, I would not have left.
02.why: Rabbi Yohanan has just said it is fortunate never to have seen one's parents, so hard is it to honor them properly; Rav Asi's story shows that strain, and the Gemara then turns to how one honors a parent in life and in death.

people.name: Rav Asi
people.about: A Sage whose elderly mother made demands he could not meet; he left for the Land of Israel.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: The Sage Rav Asi asked whether he could leave the Land of Israel to meet his mother.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar
people.about: A Sage who told Rav Asi that Rabbi Yohanan's words were a blessing, not a sign of anger.

terms.meaning: The Land of Israel. Leaving it for other lands was considered prohibited without a good reason.
A name for God, literally 'the Place', used in blessings and prayers.

03.note: At his son's wedding celebration, Rava himself served drinks to the guests. When he poured a cup for Rav Pappa and Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua, they stood up before him. When he poured for Rav Mari and Rav Pinehas son of Rav Hisda, they did not stand. Rava became angry and said: Are these rabbis real Sages, and those not Sages?
03.why: Rav Yosef and Rava have said that a teacher who waives the honor due to him has it waived. The Gemara raises this story as a challenge: Rava served his guests, yet was angry when Sages did not stand for him.

people.name: Rava
people.about: A Sage who served drinks at his son's wedding and was angered when two guests did not stand for him.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: A guest at the wedding who stood when Rava poured for him.

people.name: Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua
people.about: A guest who stood when Rava poured for him.

people.name: Rav Mari
people.about: A guest who did not stand for Rava.

people.name: Rav Pinehas son of Rav Hisda
people.about: A guest who did not stand for Rava.

04.note: At the wedding celebration of his son Abba Mar, Rav Pappa served drinks to the guests. When he poured a cup for Rav Yitzhak son of Rav Yehuda, the guest did not stand up before him, and Rav Pappa became angry.
04.why: This is a second challenge, after Rava's wedding, to the view that a teacher can waive his honor. The Gemara answers that even when he waives it, others must still show him some act of reverence.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: A Sage who served drinks at his son's wedding and was angered when a guest did not stand.

people.name: Abba Mar
people.about: Rav Pappa's son, whose wedding it was.

people.name: Rav Yitzhak son of Rav Yehuda
people.about: A guest who did not stand when Rav Pappa poured for him.

05.note: Rabbi Eliezer, Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Tzadok were reclining at the wedding feast of Rabban Gamliel's son, and Rabban Gamliel, the head of the Sanhedrin, stood and served them drinks. Rabbi Eliezer would not take the cup; Rabbi Yehoshua took it. Rabbi Eliezer protested: we sit while Rabban Gamliel stands and serves us? Rabbi Yehoshua answered that Abraham, a greater man, served his guests, who looked to him like ordinary Arabs, not angels. Rabbi Tzadok said: How long will you ignore God's honor? God makes the winds blow, brings the rain and sets a table for every creature; should not Rabban Gamliel serve us?
05.why: Rav Ashi has said that even if a rabbi may waive his honor, a Nasi may not. The Gemara cites this incident against him, since the Nasi served and the Sages accepted; afterward Rav Ashi's rule is restated as applying to a king.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel
people.about: The Nasi, who served drinks at his son's wedding.

people.name: Rabbi Eliezer
people.about: A guest who refused the cup from Rabban Gamliel.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua
people.about: A guest who accepted the cup and defended doing so by citing Abraham.

people.name: Rabbi Tzadok
people.about: A guest who argued from God's care for every creature.

people.name: Abraham
people.about: The forefather, cited as a great man who stood over his guests and served them.

terms.meaning: The president of the Sanhedrin, the highest Jewish court, and leader of the Jewish community.
At formal meals guests ate leaning on couches; the host or servants stood and served them.

06.note: Bar Kappara (some say it was Rabbi Shmuel bar Rabbi Yosei) was sitting in a bathhouse when Rabbi Shimon, son of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, came in and passed by, and he did not stand up for him. Rabbi Shimon was angry and went to complain to his father: I taught him two of the nine parts of Torat Kohanim, and he did not stand for me. His father answered: Perhaps he was sitting and thinking over what you taught him.
06.why: A teaching said one need not stand for an elder in a bathhouse. The Gemara cites this story as a challenge: the father excused the student only because he was lost in thought, implying one must stand even there.

people.name: Bar Kappara
people.about: The man sitting in the bathhouse who did not stand; some say it was Rabbi Shmuel bar Rabbi Yosei.

people.name: Rabbi Shmuel bar Rabbi Yosei
people.about: Named in another version as the one who did not stand.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon bar Rabbi
people.about: Son of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi; he had taught the man and was angry not to be honored.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: Rabbi Shimon's father, who suggested the man had been lost in thought.

terms.meaning: An early collection of rabbinic interpretation of the book of Leviticus, divided into parts.

07.note: Abaye used to stand up as soon as he saw the ear of Rav Yosef's donkey coming toward him. Once Abaye was riding a donkey along the bank of the Sagya River, and Rav Mesharshiyya and other rabbis sitting on the other bank did not stand for him. Abaye said to them: Am I not your primary teacher? They answered: It did not enter our minds, which the translation takes to mean they had not seen him.
07.why: Abaye has just ruled that one stands for an ordinary elder only within four cubits, but for one's primary teacher as soon as he comes into view; both incidents show that rule in practice.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: A Sage who stood for his teacher from afar and expected the same from his students.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: The Sage whose approaching donkey Abaye would stand for.

people.name: Rav Mesharshiyya
people.about: One of the rabbis on the far bank who did not stand for Abaye.

terms.meaning: The teacher from whom a person learned most of his Torah, owed greater honor than other Sages.

08.note: Ravina was sitting before Rabbi Yirmeya of Difti when a man passed in front of him without covering his head. Ravina said: How rude this man is. Rabbi Yirmeya answered: Perhaps he is from Mata Mehasya, where rabbis are common.
08.why: The discussion is about the respect owed to Sages and teachers; Rabbi Yirmeya suggests that someone used to seeing rabbis every day may not show it, so the lapse need not be rudeness.

people.name: Ravina
people.about: A Sage who called a passer-by rude for not covering his head.

people.name: Rabbi Yirmeya of Difti
people.about: The Sage Ravina was sitting before, who defended the passer-by.

terms.meaning: A sign of respect; the man was expected to cover his head when passing a rabbi.

09.note: Rav Hanan and Rav Anan were traveling on a road and saw a man sowing different kinds of seeds together. One said to the other: Let the Master come and let us ostracize him. The other replied that he did not understand these laws. Then they saw a man sowing wheat and barley between grapevines, and again one wanted to ostracize him. The other answered that they follow Rabbi Yoshiya, who says a person is liable only if he sows wheat, barley and a grape seed in a single throw.
09.why: The Gemara has just said that the ban on sowing mixed seeds applies only in the Land of Israel, while grafting different trees is banned everywhere; this story shows Sages declining to punish a man for mixed sowing.

people.name: Rav Hanan
people.about: One of two Sages traveling together who came upon men sowing mixed seeds.

people.name: Rav Anan
people.about: His traveling companion.

people.name: Rabbi Yoshiya
people.about: A Sage whose opinion on when mixed sowing makes one liable is cited.

terms.meaning: To place someone under a ban, cutting him off from the community as a punishment.
The Torah's prohibition on mixing species: sowing different seeds together, planting grain in a vineyard, grafting trees or crossbreeding animals.

10.note: One account of how Aher went astray: he saw the tongue of Hutzpit the disseminator, who, as the translation explains, had been executed by the government, being dragged along by 'something else', a euphemism for a pig. Aher said: Shall a mouth that produced pearls lick the dust? And he went out and sinned.
10.why: Rav Yosef said Aher would not have sinned had he read the Torah's promise of reward as referring to the World-to-Come. The Gemara asks what made him sin and gives this as a second answer, after the boy who died doing a mitzva.

people.name: Aher
people.about: Literally 'Other', the name given to the Sage Elisha ben Avuya after he abandoned the Torah.

people.name: Hutzpit the disseminator
people.about: A Sage whose tongue Aher saw dragged in the dirt after his death.

terms.meaning: The speaker who repeated and explained a Sage's lecture aloud to the audience.

11.note: A noblewoman tried to seduce Rabbi Hanina bar Pappi. He said a formula and covered himself with boils and scabs; she performed an act of magic and he was healed. He fled and hid in a bathhouse so dangerous that even two people entering together by day would be harmed. The next day the Sages asked who had protected him. He said two of the emperor's guards had watched over him all night (angels, in the translation's reading). They said: Perhaps a forbidden sexual relationship came your way and you were saved from it, for a miracle is done for anyone who resists such a temptation.
11.why: Rava has just explained that one who 'sits and does not sin' is rewarded when a chance to sin comes to him and he resists it; this story illustrates such a person.

people.name: Rabbi Hanina bar Pappi
people.about: A Sage who resisted a noblewoman's advances and was protected overnight in a dangerous bathhouse.

terms.meaning: Matronita, a Roman lady of rank; in these stories a powerful woman who tempts a Sage.

12.note: A noblewoman tried to seduce Rabbi Tzadok. He told her his heart was weak and he could not, and asked for something to eat. She said she had only non-kosher food. He said: What difference does it make? One who does this act may eat this food. She lit the oven to roast it, and he climbed in and sat in the oven. When she asked what this meant, he said: One who does that act falls into this fire. She said: Had I known it was so serious for you, I would not have caused you such anguish.
12.why: The Sages have just taught that a miracle is done for whoever escapes a forbidden sexual temptation, and cited a verse about 'mighty' people such as Rabbi Tzadok and his colleagues; this is the story that phrase refers to.

people.name: Rabbi Tzadok
people.about: A Sage who escaped a noblewoman's advances by sitting in her lit oven.

terms.meaning: The place of punishment for the wicked after death, pictured as fire; the translation says this is the fire Rabbi Tzadok meant.

13.note: Rav Kahana sold baskets, and a noblewoman tried to seduce him. He told her he would go and make himself ready, then went up to the roof and threw himself down toward the ground. Elijah the prophet came and caught him, and said: You made me travel four hundred parasangs. Rav Kahana answered: What brought me to this, if not poverty? Elijah gave him a basket full of dinars.
13.why: It is the last in a series of stories about Sages who resisted seduction and were saved by a miracle, illustrating the teaching that whoever escapes a forbidden sexual temptation has a miracle done for him.

people.name: Rav Kahana
people.about: A poor Sage who sold baskets and threw himself from a roof to escape a noblewoman.

people.name: Elijah
people.about: The prophet, who caught Rav Kahana in midair and gave him money.

terms.meaning: A Persian measure of distance, a few miles; four hundred parasangs is a very long journey.
A coin; a basket full of them was a fortune.

14.note: A husband and wife disagreed over whom to marry their young daughter to: he wanted his relative, she wanted hers. She pressed him until he said: Let her be for your relative. But while they were eating and drinking at the meal, his relative came onto the roof and betrothed the girl to himself.
14.why: The Gemara is asking when a minor betrothed without her father's consent is still betrothed because he secretly wanted it. Abaye says this father kept his word to his wife; Rava says no one prepares a feast and then lets it go to waste.

terms.meaning: The first stage of Jewish marriage, done by giving the woman (or a minor girl's father) money or an object of value; for a minor, it depends on her father's wish.

15.note: A man sold his property, stating that he meant to move to the Land of Israel. He went up but could not settle there. Rava ruled that whoever goes up intends to settle, and since he could not, the sale can be cancelled. Another version reports that Rava said the opposite: he meant to go up, and he went up, so the sale stands.
15.why: The Gemara has just argued that unspoken intentions do not count in a transaction. Here the seller stated his reason aloud, and the question becomes how far that stated purpose reaches.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The Sage who ruled on the sale; two versions of his ruling are reported.

terms.meaning: The Land of Israel; 'going up' is the usual way to speak of moving there.

16.note: A man sold his property intending to move to the Land of Israel, but in the end he did not go. Rav Ashi said: If he had wanted, he could have gone up, so the sale stands. Another version gives his words as a question: If he had wanted, could he not have gone up?
16.why: It follows the case of a seller who went but could not settle. The Gemara explains that the two versions of Rav Ashi's words differ over a man stopped on the way by circumstances beyond his control.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: The Sage who ruled on the sale; two versions of his words are reported.

terms.meaning: The Land of Israel; 'going up' is the usual way to speak of moving there.

17.note: After Rabbi Meir died, Rabbi Yehuda told his students not to let Rabbi Meir's students in, calling them quarrelsome men who came not to learn but to overwhelm him with laws. Sumakhos, a student of Rabbi Meir, pushed his way in and reported Rabbi Meir's teaching that a priest who betroths a woman with his share of the offerings has not betrothed her. Rabbi Yehuda grew angry, repeated his warning, and objected that a woman is never in the Temple courtyard. Rabbi Yosei said: People will say Meir died, Yehuda grew angry and Yosei was silent; what will become of the Torah? He answered that a father can accept betrothal for his daughter there, a woman can send an agent, and she might push in.
17.why: The mishna rules that a priest cannot betroth a woman with his portion of the offerings; this teaching gives that ruling as Rabbi Meir taught it, and the Gemara goes on to the dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yosei.

people.name: Rabbi Meir
people.about: A Sage who had died; his teaching is reported by his student.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda
people.about: A Sage who barred Rabbi Meir's students from his study hall.

people.name: Sumakhos
people.about: A student of Rabbi Meir who pushed his way in.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei
people.about: A Sage present who answered Rabbi Yehuda's objection.

terms.meaning: The parts of sacrificed animals given to priests to eat. Some, of the most sacred order, could be eaten only inside the Temple courtyard.
To perform the first stage of marriage, usually by giving the woman money or an object of value.
The inner area of the Temple in Jerusalem where sacrifices were offered and the holiest portions eaten.

18.note: Shimon HaAmasoni (some say Nehemya HaAmasoni) used to draw a teaching from every 'et' in the Torah. When he reached the verse 'You shall fear et the Lord your God', he stopped, since, as the translation explains, nothing can be feared alongside God. His students asked: What will become of all the 'et's you have interpreted? He said: Just as I was rewarded for interpreting, I am rewarded for withdrawing. This stood until Rabbi Akiva came and taught that the 'et' in that verse includes Torah scholars.
18.why: The Gemara has just said that one Sage does not draw laws from the word 'et', and cites this teaching to show that this was a real method of reading that a Sage could give up.

people.name: Shimon HaAmasoni
people.about: A Sage who drew teachings from every 'et' in the Torah, then withdrew; some name him Nehemya HaAmasoni.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: A Sage who later read the 'et' in 'You shall fear the Lord your God' as including Torah scholars.

terms.meaning: A small Hebrew word that marks the object of a verb and has no meaning of its own; some Sages read it as adding something extra to a verse.

19.note: Rav Giddel was negotiating for a plot of land when Rabbi Abba bought it. Rav Giddel complained to Rabbi Zeira, who took it to Rav Yitzhak Nappaha, who said to wait for the Festival visit. Then he asked Rabbi Abba: If a poor man is reaching for a loaf and another takes it, what is he? Wicked, said Rabbi Abba. Then why did you do it? I did not know, he said. He refused to sell, since it was his first land and selling it was a bad omen, but offered it as a gift. Rav Giddel would not take a gift, citing 'he who hates gifts shall live', and Rabbi Abba would not use it because Rav Giddel had wanted it. Neither took it, and it was called the land of the Sages.
19.why: The Gemara has been telling of agents who bought for themselves what they were sent to get for another; this story extends the theme to someone who takes a deal another person is already pursuing.

people.name: Rav Giddel
people.about: A Sage negotiating for a plot of land when another bought it.

people.name: Rabbi Abba
people.about: The Sage who bought the land without knowing Rav Giddel wanted it.

people.name: Rabbi Zeira
people.about: The Sage Rav Giddel complained to.

people.name: Rav Yitzhak Nappaha
people.about: The Sage who confronted Rabbi Abba about the purchase.

terms.meaning: One of the three festivals (Passover, Shavuot, Sukkot) when people traveled to gather and hear the Sages' public lectures.

20.note: A blind man used to recite mishnayot before Mar Shmuel. One day he was late, and Mar Shmuel sent a messenger after him. The messenger went one way and the blind man arrived by another. When the messenger came back, he said that the blind man's wife had committed adultery. The blind man came to Mar Shmuel, who told him: If he is trusted by you, go and divorce her; if not, do not divorce her.
20.why: The Sages asked whether one witness is believed when he tells a husband his wife committed adultery and the husband is silent. Abaye says yes and cites this case; Rava reads Mar Shmuel as meaning trusted like two witnesses.

people.name: Mar Shmuel
people.about: The Sage who advised the blind man after the messenger's report.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: A Sage who holds one witness is believed and cites this case as proof.

people.name: Rava
people.about: A Sage who holds one witness is not enough in matters of forbidden relations.

terms.meaning: Plural of mishna: the short teachings of the early Sages, which students recited from memory before a teacher.
Jewish law usually requires two witnesses to establish a fact; the question is whether one is enough here.
